Aristote décrit déjà ce piège dans les R: Aristotle already described this trap in the Sophistical Refutations, in the 4th century BC, as the fallacy "connected with the consequent": snow and the swan are both white, but they are not the same thing.
Le premier à décrire explicitement ce ra: The first to describe this reasoning explicitly, "if A then B; not B; therefore not A", was Theophrastus, Aristotle's pupil. Today it is called modus tollens.
Aristote distingue déjà, dans De l'inter: Aristotle already distinguished, in On Interpretation, "every man is white" from its contradictory "not every man is white". Boethius later drew the famous square of opposition from it.
George Boole, mathématicien autodidacte,: George Boole, a self-taught mathematician, put logic into equations in 1847 and then in 1854 in The Laws of Thought. In 1937, Claude Shannon showed that this algebra could be used to design circuits: the basis of computers.
Aristote définit le syllogisme dans les: Aristotle defined the syllogism in the Prior Analytics, around 350 BC. His logic dominated Western thought for centuries; in the Middle Ages, this very argument was memorised under the name "Barbara".
Augustus De Morgan énonce ces lois en 18: Augustus De Morgan stated these laws in 1847 in his Formal Logic. But Aristotle had made a similar remark, and William of Ockham was already writing them out in words in the 14th century.
Cette définition de « si… alors » vient: This definition of "if... then" comes from Philo the Dialectician, around 300 BC: a conditional is false only if the antecedent is true and the consequent false. It is the one used in modern logic.
Les logiciens du Moyen Âge donnaient un: Medieval logicians gave a name to each valid form of syllogism, whose vowels encoded the type of proposition: Barbara, Celarent, Darii... A way to learn them by heart.
Wittgenstein popularise les tables de vé: Wittgenstein popularised truth tables in the Tractatus, published in 1921, and Emil Post proposed them the same year. But Charles Sanders Peirce was already drawing them in manuscripts from 1883-1884.
L'exemple le plus célèbre est la preuve: The most famous example is the proof that √2 is not a fraction, which Aristotle already alludes to. According to legend, Hippasus of Metapontum was killed for revealing this discovery.
Les Romains croyaient que les cygnes noi: The Romans believed black swans did not exist: the poet Juvenal speaks of a bird "as rare as a black swan". In 1697, explorer Willem de Vlamingh saw some in Australia.
La phrase d'Épiménide, vers 600 avant no: Epimenides' line, around 600 BC, is quoted in the Epistle to Titus without any problem being seen in it. Only with Bertrand Russell, in 1908, was it presented as "the oldest contradiction of the kind".
Le papyrus Rhind, vers 1550 avant notre: The Rhind papyrus, around 1550 BC, already contains first-degree equations, the "aha" problems: for example x + x/3 + x/4 = 2. It was bought near Luxor in 1858 by Alexander Rhind.
Le traité d'al-Khwârizmî est traduit en: Al-Khwarizmi's treatise was translated into Latin by Robert of Chester in 1145. It remained a textbook in European universities until the 16th century, even though everything in it is written in words, with no symbols at all.
Diophante d'Alexandrie, au IIIe siècle,: Diophantus of Alexandria, in the 3rd century, was one of the first to use a symbol for the unknown. It was in the margin of a 1621 edition of his Arithmetica that Fermat wrote his famous "last theorem".
Le mot « imaginaire » pour ces nombres v: The word "imaginary" for these numbers comes from Descartes, and it was Euler who introduced the letter i. Electrical engineers often write j, because for them i means current.
Le chapitre 8 des Neuf Chapitres, livre: Chapter 8 of The Nine Chapters, a Chinese book compiled between the 10th and 2nd centuries BC, solves systems with up to five unknowns. Its method, fangcheng, is what we now call Gaussian elimination.
Avocat et conseiller d'Henri IV, Viète c: A lawyer and adviser to Henry IV, Viète broke a Spanish secret code of more than 500 characters in 1590. The King of Spain accused him of using magical powers.
Dès 2000 avant notre ère, des tablettes: As early as 2000 BC, Babylonian tablets solved problems about the areas of rectangles with a method equivalent to our formula. Brahmagupta gave the first explicit solution in 628.
Le signe = est inventé en 1557 par le Ga: The = sign was invented in 1557 by the Welshman Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines because "noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle". It did not appear in print again until 1618.
Niccolò Fontana doit son surnom de Tarta: Niccolò Fontana owed his nickname Tartaglia, "the stammerer", to a sabre blow from a French soldier he received as a child during the sack of Brescia in 1512, which left him with a speech impediment.
L'idée de médiane apparaît déjà dans le: The idea of the median already appears in the Talmud in the 6th century, to settle diverging appraisals. The word "median" was fixed by Francis Galton in 1881, after he had tried "middle-most value" and "medium".
En 1668, un auteur signant « D. B. » exp: In 1668, an author signing "D. B." explained in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions how he took the mean of five measurements of magnetic variation.
L'expression « écart type » est employée: The term "standard deviation" was first used in writing by Karl Pearson in 1894. Before him, Gauss spoke of "mean error".
Le mot « mode » en statistique vient aus: The word "mode" in statistics also comes from Karl Pearson, in 1895: he found it "convenient" for the value of maximum frequency.
Abraham de Moivre découvre la courbe en: Abraham de Moivre discovered the bell curve in 1733, approximating the outcomes of coin tosses. Gauss and Laplace developed it around 1809-1823; the name "normal" was popularised by Pearson in the late 19th century.
Quetelet n'avait pas conçu son indice co: Quetelet had not designed his index as a medical tool. It was in 1972 that physiologist Ancel Keys renamed it "body mass index".
Les intervalles de confiance, qui donnen: Confidence intervals, which give an estimate its margin of error, were theorised by the Pole Jerzy Neyman, in a 1934 paper and then a full account in 1937.
Le Literary Digest avait interrogé ses l: The Literary Digest had polled its readers, car owners and telephone users, wealthier than average. Roosevelt won every state but two, and the magazine folded in 1938.
En 1859, Florence Nightingale devient la: In 1859, Florence Nightingale became the first female member of the Royal Statistical Society. She called her circular diagrams "coxcombs".
C'est la proposition 32 du livre I des É: It is Proposition 32 of Book I of Euclid's Elements, already known to the Pythagoreans. In the 1820s, Gauss reportedly measured a triangle formed by three mountain peaks to check whether space really followed this rule.
Archimède démontre vers 260 avant notre: Archimedes proved around 260 BC, in Measurement of a Circle, that the area of a disc equals that of a right triangle whose base is the circumference and whose height is the radius: that is πr².
La première table trigonométrique connue: The first known trigonometric table is due to the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, in the 2nd century BC: a table of chords, in steps of 7.5°. He is nicknamed the "father of trigonometry".
« Sinus » vient d'une erreur de lecture: "Sine" comes from a misreading: the Sanskrit jyā, "bowstring", was transcribed jība in Arabic, read as jayb, "fold", and translated into Latin as sinus in the 12th century. The word "cosine" dates from 1620.
Le théorème qui relie cet excès d'angles: The theorem linking this angle excess to the triangle's area is named after Albert Girard. Thomas Harriot had proved it as early as 1603, without publishing it.
Doubler le volume d'un cube est l'un des: Doubling the volume of a cube is one of the great Greek problems, linked by legend to an oracle consulted against a plague on Delos. Pierre Wantzel proved in 1837 that it cannot be done with ruler and compass.
Thalès de Milet est né vers 625 avant no: Thales of Miletus was born around 625 BC. According to Plutarch, his shadow method pleased the pharaoh Amasis; some historians doubt, however, that such anecdotes have any value.
Le symbole π est utilisé pour la premièr: The symbol π was first used in 1706 by the Welshman William Jones, then popularised by Euler. A Babylonian tablet from 1900-1600 BC already used 3.125.
Archimède est tué en 212 avant notre ère: Archimedes was killed in 212 BC by a Roman soldier when Syracuse fell, despite General Marcellus's order to spare him. The famous "do not disturb my circles" appears in no ancient source.
Le lien entre sommets, arêtes et faces (: The link between vertices, edges and faces (8 - 12 + 6 = 2 for the cube) was stated by Euler in 1758. Francesco Maurolico had noted it as early as 1537 for the Platonic solids, in an unpublished manuscript.
Gauss avait trouvé les idées de la géomé: Gauss had found the ideas of non-Euclidean geometry around 1813, but never published them. A century earlier, in 1733, Saccheri had brushed against it while believing he was proving Euclid's postulate.
Archimède utilise une somme de ce genre: Archimedes used a sum of this kind in the 3rd century BC to calculate the area under a parabola. Euclid had already given the sum of a finite geometric sequence, in Book IX of the Elements.
Galilée remarque dès 1638, dans ses Deux: Galileo noted as early as 1638, in his Two New Sciences, that there are as many squares as whole numbers. He concluded that "more", "less" and "equal" do not apply to infinity: Cantor would show otherwise.
Zénon d'Élée, vers 490-430 avant notre è: Zeno of Elea, around 490-430 BC, wanted to defend his teacher Parmenides, for whom motion is an illusion. His texts are lost: we know his paradoxes through Aristotle's Physics.
Son ancien professeur Leopold Kronecker: His former professor Leopold Kronecker called Cantor a "corrupter of youth". David Hilbert defended him: "No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created."
Le Liber abaci de 1202 sert surtout à fa: The 1202 Liber abaci mainly served to introduce Hindu-Arabic numerals and place value to Europe. The sequence existed before Fibonacci: it only owes him its name.
Euclide appelait ce nombre le partage en: Euclid called this number the division in "extreme and mean ratio", and Luca Pacioli the "divine proportion". The link with the Fibonacci sequence was noticed by Simon Jacob, then by Kepler.
La preuve d'Oresme, vers 1350, tombe dan: Oresme's proof, around 1350, fell into obscurity. Pietro Mengoli redid it in 1650, and Jacob Bernoulli published another in 1689, crediting it to his brother Johann.
David Hilbert présente son hôtel dans un: David Hilbert presented his hotel in a 1924-1925 lecture, "On the Infinite". It was George Gamow's book One Two Three... Infinity, in 1947, that made it famous.
Le problème 79 du papyrus Rhind, vers 15: Problem 79 of the Rhind papyrus, around 1550 BC, is already a geometric sequence: 7 houses, 49 cats, 343 mice, 2,401 spelt plants, 16,807 measures of grain.
Wallis n'a jamais expliqué pourquoi il a: Wallis never explained why he chose this sign. One hypothesis links it to an old Roman way of writing 1,000, CIↃ; another to the Greek letter omega.
Euler justifie déjà que 0,999… = 1 dans: Euler already justified that 0.999... = 1 in his Elements of Algebra, in 1770. The rigorous definitions of real numbers that settle the question arrived in 1872.
Newton développe ses « fluxions » dès 16: Newton developed his "fluxions" from 1666 but published nothing; Leibniz published first, in 1684. The Royal Society report that ruled in Newton's favour, in 1712, was written by Newton himself.
